💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority.
  • Industry observers note that protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority. The reason isn’t quantum computers.

Industry observers note that protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters. The quantum threat has always been a hardware problem, and hardware problems announce themselves years in advance because somebody has to build the machine. The AI version is a math problem. A sufficiently capable model could find a structural shortcut in the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin, and it would need no special hardware to do it.

Researcher Justin Drake raised the scenario in October. In a worst case, he noted, existing signatures could become vulnerable within months.

Recent findings suggest that an Anthropic mathematician named Levent Alpöge posted a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with an unreleased version of Claude, along with a formalized proof archive. Nobody has verified it. It doesn’t break elliptic curve cryptography and nobody is claiming it does. What it does is demonstrate the capability class Drake was describing, roughly a month after he described it.

Axios reported Tuesday that more than two dozen people familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic say employees worry their most advanced unreleased models may never be safe enough to release. The concerns named include reward hacking, models that hide or misrepresent their reasoning, and systems capable enough to find weaknesses in the safety measures their own developers built. OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed Sunday that labs agree on shared limits on how far they train models.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The plan replaces elliptic curves with hash-based cryptography, which rests on fewer structural assumptions about mathematics. It touches how consumers authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how layer-2 data gets verified. Drake proposed pulling the deadline from December 2029 to December 2028. Ethlabs withdrew its faster-block-production proposal from the Hegotá upgrade to free up engineers. The Foundation has deployed AI agents to hunt bugs in its own infrastructure, which is a reasonable response and also an admission about where the advantage currently sits.

Wedderburn’s own framing: it’s harder than the Merge, and there’s less time. He also acknowledged that moving faster makes it easier to ship bugs.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin is on the same road. Blockstream’s Jonas Nick published a security analysis of SHRINCS last week, the apparent frontrunner to replace Bitcoin’s signatures, with sizes running from 548 bytes to 5,777 against today’s 64 to 71.

Sources indicate that so the AI threat is looming (and accelerating), but the two largest crypto assets have teams that are responding. Now we wait on action, and more assurances that crypto is safe from AI threats. Assurances that could ensure the bottom is in fact in, if and when they arrive….

Coinbase has suspended trading for 12 crypto trading pairs, including those of Cardano (ADA) and Stellar (XLM), as November 2026 wraps up with just a few days left.

Industry observers note that the delisting took place on November 25, as Coinbase revealed earlier. The affected pairs include APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, XLM-BTC, ICP-BTC, and ADA-ETH, among others.

The full list includes APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP, and SNX-GBP, with trading suspended across Coinbase Exchange, Advanced Trade and Coinbase Prime.

Coinbase regularly monitors the markets on the exchange and, in an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity, has removed a number of non-USD trading pairs for supported assets.

In similar delisting news, Coinbase has disabled trading for Stargate Finance (STG), Vulcan Forged (PYR), Neon EVM (NEON), and Syndicate (SYND), in line with the shake-up on its platform in November. People' funds will remain accessible, and users will be able to withdraw them at any time.

As stated earlier, Coinbase regularly monitors the markets on the exchange and might delist some assets to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity.

Based on recent reviews, Coinbase will suspend trading for Centrifuge (CFG) on December 18, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Centrifuge has separately unveiled it is ending token support for CFG and allowing holders to convert CFG tokens into equity in Centrifuge.

According to recent reports, also in December, Coinbase will be performing a system upgrade. In an X post, the exchange stated it has scheduled a system upgrade for Saturday, December 5, 2026, around 7 a.m. PT, estimated to last about 4 hours.

During this time, Coinbase stated that all trading and transfers will be unavailable, and the Coinbase Exchange will be temporarily offline. Owners are advised to take note and prepare accordingly so as to avoid any delays on that date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Recent findings suggest that huawei believes its fresh Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

According to recent reports, the Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” stated Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”.

According to recent reports, huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

Recent findings suggest that if that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

According to recent reports, alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! Hedera [HBAR] has rallied 8.96% in 24 hours, alongside a modest 2.6% Bitcoin [BTC] bounce from its $57.3k low on Wednesday. Hedera’s token price bounce was one of the biggest among the top 35 crypto assets by market capitalization.

According to recent reports, there was no direct catalyst or coin-specific development that helped Hedera post its heavy short-term gains. Rather, the price could be moving from one pocket of liquidity to another, aided by Bitcoin’s bounce.

In a recent development, the 2-week liquidation heatmap highlighted $0.0480-$0.0493 as a nearby cluster of long liquidations. The selling pressure saw HBAR decline from its $0.056 Monday peak.

After sweeping the $0.048 liquidity pocket, which was also around the $0.048 local low HBAR token made last week, the altcoin has rallied 11.3%.

Industry observers note that this was a strong price reaction. CoinMarketCap data revealed a 26% daily trading volume increase, showing demand backed the short-term gains.

To the north, the $0.057 zone was a strong magnetic zone. A denser cluster of liquidity gathered around $0.06, the local supply zone. It appeared likely that HBAR was preparing to test these resistance zones.

While the short-term momentum and sizeable bullish relative strength against Bitcoin were tempting, buyers should remain cautious. The price trend on the 1-day timeframe was bearish.

In particular, the magnetic zones highlighted earlier at $0.057 and $0.06 were close to the local swing points from earlier this month, at $0.0548 and $0.0594.

It is highly likely that an HBAR foray into these zones would result in a setback as underwater and short-term holders rush to exit their positions.

The OBV was in a deep downtrend and revealed steady selling pressure in recent weeks. A pause in this downtrend would be a good sign for investors looking to buy.

Until $0.059 is breached and the OBV begins to reverse, swing traders and investors can maintain a bearish bias.

Two XRP Ledger lending amendments, LendingProtocol and LendingProtocolV1_1, each have 28 votes out of 35 validators, or 80%, according to XRPScan data on Thursday. Each of them needs one more vote to start a 14-day countdown to activation, according to XRPScan.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, the SingleAssetVault amendment reached 29 votes. According to XRPScan, its earliest activation date is Dec. 9, and its support has to stay above 80% until then.

XRP was trading at around $0.95 on Thursday, up 4.1% over 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap.

On Nov. 20, XRPScan indicated 25 votes for SingleAssetVault and 24 votes for each of the two lending amendments. Validators run by Interledger, onXRP, GateHub and Flare were among the last to vote for them.

Industry observers note that rippleX opened LendingProtocolV1_1 for voting with a post on X on Sept. 30, when the amendment arrived with rippled version 3.4.0. "LendingProtocolV1_1 is open for validator voting. It introduces closed-ended vaults and cash-basis accounting for XRPL lending, and it must activate before LendingProtocol and SingleAssetVault can proceed," the RippleX developer account wrote.

J. Ayo Akinyele, head of engineering at RippleX, explained the role of the update in a post on June 25. "v1.1 is an enhancement to the Lending Protocol, not a replacement for v1.0," he wrote, adding that "Lending on XRPL will evolve dynamically.".

It has been revealed that ripple described the mechanics of the protocol on Nov. 19. "The upcoming XRP Ledger Lending Protocol is designed to bring loan issuance and repayment directly onto the ledger. Lenders deposit into a Single Asset Vault, and the Lending Protocol lets loan brokers use that capital to problem loans and track repayments onchain," the firm wrote on X.

Sources indicate that ripple engineer Ed Hennis presented the protocol in a thread on X in December 2025. He called it a protocol-native system for "fixed-term, fixed-rate, underwritten credit." "XRP's $124B market cap can finally be lent into institutional credit facilities to generate real yield instead of sitting idle," Hennis wrote at the time.

Jazzi Cooper, head of product at RippleX, wrote on Sept. 11 that "XRP as collateral for institutional credit is a killer use case (and supported by xls65/66 lending protocol!)".

On the same day, the XRP Ledger Foundation shared an interview with its chief technology officer, Denis Angell. "We are writing TradFi primitives into the XRP Ledger," Angell noted. In the interview, he compared the lending protocol to a closed-end fund, where investors put in XRP or RLUSD and receive interest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

In a recent development, originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

Sources indicate that in other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a substantial tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

It has been revealed that to be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

According to recent reports, there are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis prepares to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#144699. Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2287 w)
📖 Baca

Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning.
  • That’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo.
  • Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning. She’s loved music her whole life and was always drawn to EDM, but marrying and having kids young left little room to explore it. Then, three years ago, her husband died, and she began thinking about how short and precious life is—and decided it was time to push herself to try newly introduced experiences.

That’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo. She was nervous, but spent the night dancing, and left with new friends and a newfound confidence. “I felt uninhibited,” she says. She’s attended more than 20 raves since.

Manson isn’t an outlier. Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns. And a number of them are finding relief on the dance floor.

In a recent development, A 2025 study in Psychology of Music surveyed 136 women ages 40 to 65 about why they’re involved in EDM experiences. The overwhelming response was that raving was a meaningful part of their mental well-being—an outlet for stress, a source of connection, and a rare place to escape the demands of everyday life, according to the survey.

Sources indicate that “There is a rise in older people attending electronic dance music events, raves, clubs, parties, festivals,” says Alice O’Grady, PhD, a professor of applied performance at the University of Leeds, who co-authored the Psychology of Music study. “The motivations for women going are pretty much characterized as the same as they are for any age: the love of the music, the ability to socialize with existing friends, the atmosphere of the environment, and the sense of community.” Put simply: These music events are plain fun.

Sources indicate that the EDM scene is no longer the epitome of youth culture, O’Grady adds, and it’s become more socially acceptable for women to embrace this genre of joy as they get older. That shift may reflect changing attitudes about aging, with women potentially feeling less constrained by traditional expectations about how they’re “supposed” to spend their time as they age. Social media has also made it much easier to discover niche music scenes, while a growing focus on mental health, movement, pleasure, and community may be encouraging women to seek out experiences that just make them feel good.

According to recent reports, the older you get, the harder it can be to find a place where you can be playful, spontaneous, and fully present with other people. For some, the rave scene provides exactly that. “You've got more responsibility, more commitments,” O’Grady says. “You want that escape, you want that ability to connect through music and immerse yourself in an environment that allows you to be expressive and just shake off some of those roles that older women carry.”.

Industry observers note that samantha Hillery, 43, started raving in her 20s as a way to let loose and have fun. But as life got busier with work, family, and kids, she stopped going. Years later, while searching for fun things to do in her area with friends, she came across Bingo Loco, a high-energy party with EDM, dancing, confetti, and—yes—bingo, and found her way back to it.

Now, Hillery gives herself permission to step away from the endless list of adult responsibilities. “As we get older and super busy with our lives, we forget how fun we maybe used to be, and it seems like something that was so far in the past,” she indicates. “But when you’re able to go out and rave surrounded by a bunch of friends and people that just want to have a good time, you remember that part of you isn’t lost.”.

For some, keeping up with friends also becomes more challenging as you age and enter fresh eras of your life. Social obligations often come second, competing with work schedules, children, relationships, and other obligations, says Madison Liddle, LMHC, a licensed psychotherapist at Madison Liddle Therapy and co-founder of The Practice Co, a co-working space for therapists. At a music event like these, though, spontaneous connection is built into the experience.

According to recent reports, hundreds or thousands are gathered around the same music, moving to the same rhythm, creating an immediate sense of belonging. It’s a concept called collective effervescence, which is “a feeling of joy and connection when a group of people are in a shared space doing a shared thing,” Liddle explains. “Social connection is a really strong determinant of health as we age, and raving offers an opportunity to create and be in community with people with shared interests.”.

Getting out and meeting new people is the main reason Manson is so attracted to rave culture—she’s found the crowds to be welcoming and friendly. “Life can become quite small if you don't push yourself,” she says, alluding to feeling alone after her husband’s passing. “I enjoy meeting people, I enjoy conversations. I'm not good at home in my own company—I need socialization.” Dancing with new friends is the way to do that, and it keeps her feeling energized.

In fact, in Manson’s experience, the EDM scene has seemed remarkably friendly to people of all ages and backgrounds. O’Grady agrees: “Women need spaces that are inclusive, welcoming, and accessible, and the rave scene actually does that quite well,” claims O’Grady. You’ll feel a sense of belonging, like you’re part of something bigger than yourself, even if you’re there alone, she adds. The music creates an instant common language, while dancing alongside friends and strangers turns what could be an individual activity into something meaningful and collective.

The physical perks of dancing are well documented. It strengthens the cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive systems, as WH previously reported. It can also improve coordination, balance, and stability, which becomes especially crucial with age. But it can boost your mental health too, mainly because it helps you stay present. When you’re fully focused on what you’re hearing, feeling, and doing, there’s less room to get caught up in the mental replaying and worrying that can fuel stress, Liddle says.

In fact, many participants in the Psychology of Music study described dancing at raves as a way to ease anxiety, depression, and low moods, notes co-author Alinka Greasley, PhD, a professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. Anxiety can keep the mind focused on what might go wrong, while depression can make the present feel flat.

It has been revealed that raving, by contrast, demands attention in a different way. Instead of sitting with your thoughts, you’re listening to loud, immersive music, dancing to the beat, and anticipating the next drop, Liddle explains. That physical engagement helps interrupt rumination and creates a sense of clarity that lasts beyond the dance floor; it can help clear your head.

Industry observers note that alex Daly attended her first EDM show at 40 after her partner, who’d been going to raves for years, encouraged her to come along. A year later, raving has become a central part of her wellness routine. If she’s having a stressful week and doesn’t have an EDM show on her calendar, she immediately starts looking for one. “Once I’m in the crowd, I get into a flow state, and moving my body to the beat really helps me process my emotions,” says Daly, now 41. “Dancing helps me stop ruminating, get out of my head, and back into my body.” For a few hours, there’s simply less room for the mental noise of everyday life. In a way, it’s like the pounding beat is a reset button you can dance to.

Of course, rave culture has long been tied to recreational drugs like MDMA, which can bring on feelings of euphoria, connection, and stress relief. That link hasn’t disappeared. Some of the women in the Psychology of Music study said they took drugs, often to keep their energy up for dancing, while others went purely for the music and the movement.

Recent findings suggest that however, drugs weren’t what gave the women a sense of belonging, the study uncovered. “That's very much already there from their perspective,” Greasley says. “The drugs are more to do with [increasing] energy levels and also the marrying of the drugs and the music. Many women called it a spiritual experience to be in ecstatic states whilst dancing to the music.”.

It has been revealed that karen D., 62, who asked that her last name be withheld because she discusses her drug use, sees it the same way. She started going to raves in her early 50s with her second husband. While she partakes in recreational drug use, she also knows people who attend raves completely sober. For her, the bonding comes from dancing with like-minded people who are all just happy to be there.

Recent findings suggest that but Karen acknowledges that drugs heighten those feelings and add to the mental health boost she gets from raving. “I feel like my brain’s reconnecting in ways that it has forgotten how to connect,” she says. “I can get down with what’s going on in my life at times, and it completely transforms me into a much more positive person.”.

Recent findings suggest that wellness advice in your 40s, 50s, and beyond is often the same advice over and over: protect your sleep, drink less, manage stress, and stick to a routine. But in contrast, this group of ravers finds genuine self-care in the act of staying out late, dancing for hours, and disrupting those prescribed wellness rules. “In this world where everything is so optimized and planned and scheduled, there is something that we lose in terms of fun,” claims Liddle, noting that raving brings it to the forefront. The key is to accept the occasional trade-off—less sleep in the name of mental health benefits—and to strike a balance between partying and recovering.

Manson has attended a couple of Daybreaker events, which are morning, sober parties and raves, often starting around 6 a.m. Early parties like these are becoming more common. O’Grady adds that more women DJs are putting on earlier highlights with the attitude of: “We all want to get together, we all want to have a dance, but we want to be in bed by midnight.”.

However, Manson prefers later shows because she finds that’s when more traditional EDM is played. But staying up until 4 a.m. at these events has been a bit of a learning curve, so she tries to limit her events to one per weekend. “The enthusiasm's there, but I'm not prepared to spend so much time recovering,” she says. “Once is great, it does what I want it to do. It makes me feel good. I get to connect with people that I enjoy spending time with.” She prioritizes sleeping in the next morning, and just rests the next day if she needs to. Then, she can still go to the gym and take long walks during the week. (She doesn’t work anymore, so she has more flexibility to rest.).

Sources indicate that despite the missed-out-on sleep, Karen D. finds that rave life rejuvenates her. “If I've been away at a festival for a weekend, I come back very tired because I need more sleep,” she indicates. “However, I do feel refreshed somehow—more clearheaded.”.

It has been revealed that but she still makes sure to still get seven hours of sleep if she goes to bed late, so then she can still fulfill her responsibilities at home, like taking her grandson to school. The tradeoff is also worth it for her, and in fact, going to raves inadvertently benefits her wellness routine. It “really helps motivate me to do weight training, to go running, to do all these wholesome recognized exercises, because I want to stay well to be able to go and dance [until] 3 o'clock in the morning,” she notes.

Sources indicate that rave culture is no longer just for younger people, and women in midlife are soaking in every ounce of fun, freedom, community, and release. “They don't want to be defined by their age, but more importantly, they don't want to be restricted by it,” indicates O’Grady. “Saying, ‘I want to dress up in my sequins, I want to put my face on, I want to go and have a dance, I want to stay out all night and shrug off my responsibilities for a little while, I want all of that and why shouldn't I?’”.

For Manson, getting ready is part of the appeal, and she’s collected a variety of vibrant, fun outfits to go out in. “It's almost like creating a bit of an identity, which I'm quite enjoying,” she notes. At this stage of life, raving has given her a way to reinvent herself.

In a recent development, midlife can chip away at a woman’s confidence and leave her feeling overlooked. Raving pushes back on that by giving women a place to be bold and seen. As Karen D. puts it, “Women of my age can often disappear or become invisible, and it's almost the opposite of that.”.

In a recent development, since her husband’s death, Manson has made a point of pushing herself to try upcoming things. Raving has given her lasting memories, a fresh outlook, and a crew of friends who aren’t ready to stop dancing anytime soon. “I live with the feeling that life’s very short and precious,” she says, “so seize the moment.”.

The 8 Best Resistance Bands to Pack in Your Gym Bag, According to Fitness Experts

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • IF YOU WANT to gain muscle, your first instinct may be to head to the gym and hit the dumbbells.
  • Industry observers note that resistance bands are relatively affordable, lightweight, and compact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU WANT to gain muscle, your first instinct may be to head to the gym and hit the dumbbells. And while lifting will never go out of style (in our humble opinion), we're here to tell you that's not the only way to build strength. If you're short on gear—or even just want to shake things up—it's time to add some of the best resistance bands to your training arsenal.

Industry observers note that resistance bands are relatively affordable, lightweight, and compact. Most importantly, they're one of the most versatile strength accessories you can buy. Adding a resistance band into your routine can be as simple as integrating it into your bodyweight warmup, or looping it onto a kettlebell to add a little extra heat to a set of swings.

"Because of the elastic properties, resistance bands recruit muscle fibers differently than free weights," explains Juan Guadarrama, CSCS, one of the creators of Men’s Health’s "7-Minute Workouts for Fat Burn".

Of course, there are tons of different types of resistance bands (and resistance band exercises) out there, from closed loop bands, thick latex bands, and bands with handles to ones that use anchors to attach to your door. Depending on the thickness, they also provide different levels of resistance, meaning that not every band workout is for light weights.

We've spent years testing dozens of the best exercise bands of nearly every type and thickness. Men's Health fitness editors, in collaboration with Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative members Guadarrama and Eric Sung, CSCS (a trainer at Performance Lab in Fresh York City) have compared testing notes on the best resistance bands we've tried to break down what factors set the best apart from the rest.

REP Fitness’s looped bands are durable, affordable, and have a wide weight range. With resistance profiles starting as low as five pounds (3X-Light) and as high as 150 (X-Heavy), users can gradually progress any exercise over time. They’re built with layered elastic and smoothed edges to create a smoother feel as the bands stretch and to reduce the chance of fraying (which can lead to breakage). The bands are color-coded and have the weight ranges printed clearly on each band, so I instantly know what I’m grabbing.

Marketed primarily as pull-up bands, their 38-inch length makes sense for assisted bodyweight work. However, for other moves—like curls or RDLs—that length can feel unwieldy. Still, with small adjustments, such as gripping lower on the band, double-looping the band, or widening your stance to take up slack, they function just great across a wide range of exercises.

Recent findings suggest that the best value comes from REP’s five-band set (2X-Light through Heavy) at $70; it’s $50 cheaper than buying each band individually. Each band includes a one-year home-use warranty (and six months for commercial use).

Read More: The Best Items For Your Gym Bag.

Leekey’s bands cover most bases for most folks. If you’re looking for a middle-of-the-road set of looped bands to pack in your bag for travel workouts or to help with assisted pull-ups, dips, and push-ups, this is a solid choice for under $40. The brand offers many options, so carefully review the choices before selecting. With multiple bundle options available, I think the best value is one of the five-band sets with the included door anchor.

In a recent development, because Leekey isn’t completely transparent about the build quality, proceed with caution before pulling these toward your face or looping them over barbells for heavy pulls. A small percentage of reviewers reported snapping, though it’s unclear whether they overstretched the bands. Still, the product holds a 4.6-star average across more than 11,500 reviews. One customer even posted a photo of the purple bands draped over a barbell loaded with 405 pounds, writing: “I have been using these bands for added resistance on deadlifts and rack pulls. They are holding up well and help with adding resistance at the lockout of the pull.”.

Read More: The Best Resistance Band Workouts.

This set earns a spot for the sheer amount of resistance it offers—up to 300 pounds, more than any other kit on our list. That’s more than enough tension to challenge even advanced lifters. HPYGN also sells lighter-weight bundles at lower prices, but every option comes with the basics: a travel pouch, door anchor, handles, and ankle/wrist straps.

Recent findings suggest that with over 10,000 reviews and a 4.5-star average, it’s an Amazon favorite. Some users note that bands have snapped under strain or that the listed resistance feels exaggerated, though the latter is subjective. On the flip side, many reviewers praise the sturdier build. One wrote: “I was pleasantly surprised that the gear looked like the ads and worked well. I bought it because of the metal carabiners that make it easy to change bands, and I wasn’t disappointed.”.

You’ll need a solid anchor point to get the most out of these, and long-term durability is a question mark. Still, if you’re trying to ditch your gym membership or want a heavy-duty band system for travel, HPYGN’s kit is a worthy pick. It’s affordable, versatile, and capable of potentially replacing machines and free weights.

This rig gives you a little more than just the bands. We put this setup to the test, and found it to be super fun and intuitive to use. You can think of the Gorilla Bow as a hybrid tool that combines the benefits of resistance bands with a bow-style bar, which allows for a lot more versatility than a resistance band alone.

It has been revealed that the unique bow design accommodates up to 300 pounds of resistance (just to start, you can get heavier models) that you can use to target just about every muscle group. The bow itself is made out of aircraft aluminum while the resistance bands are double-wall latex, resulting in a durable, lightweight, and portable build.

Resistance is adjustable, with the bow supporting up to four bands at a time so you can customize your resistance to meet your needs. The set comes with one original 56-inch bow, four Gorilla Bands (10, 20, 30 and 50-pounds), a band wrap, and a 30-day all-access membership to Gorilla Bow's virtual training platform. It's pricey, yes. But it packs a lot more usability than your average standalone resistance band.

According to recent reports, mini bands are a staple for warm-ups and recovery work, often wrapped around the knees for lateral walks or used to cue better glute and abductor activation during squats. Titan’s version is a little different. Designed initially as attachments for the brand’s Vice Grip Trainer, these bands double as standalone mini bands. And because they’re built for machine resistance, they’re thicker, more durable, and provide far greater tension than typical minis.

The resistance ranges from 15 pounds up to 120 pounds, which means the lightest bands are great for activation drills, while the heavy green band can push your lateral walks well past warm-up territory.

The catch is price. At nearly $50, these cost significantly more than most mini-band sets, and their uses are inherently limited compared to looped or tube bands. Still, the build quality is excellent, and the extra resistance opens the door for more challenging work than you’ll get with cheaper, flimsier bands. If you’re willing to invest once for a set that won’t wear out promptly, Titan’s mini bands are a “buy once, cry once” purchase.

Rogue is synonymous with quality in the fitness equipment space, and its tube resistance bands live up to the reputation. If you’re looking for bands to actually build workouts around—not just warm up with—these are among the best. The textured rubber handles stand out: they’re coated in a knurl-like pattern that gives you a secure grip, even when your hands get sweaty.

I noted that REP Fitness’s loop bands were long at 38 inches, and Rogue’s bands clock even longer at an elastic length of 48 inches. However, the length does allow you to perform overhead presses, lateral raises, and kickbacks with the bands. To increase the tension, loop the band around a squat rack or pole and take a few steps back. (Though Rogue warns users not to overstretch the band.) Each band is a standalone product, so you can’t clip multiple elastic tubes to a pair of handles, as with other models.

Price-wise, individual bands cost a bit more than some competitors, but Rogue makes up for it with bundle pricing. A light set (bands 0-2) runs $36.50, the heavy set (3-5) is $45, and the full collection is $75. Considering the quality and the savings versus buying separately, the sets are where the real value lies. For those who want tube bands tough enough for serious training, Rogue delivers.

These resistance bands feature four tubes braided together to create a durable workout tool that can stand up to your toughest sessions. We love that users can choose from five resistance levels, ranging from feather-light to heavy-duty, and select the perfect size and tension based on their preferences and fitness level. We found the handles comfortable, featuring a protective sleeve and grommet reinforcement which helps to ensure a solid grip.

Sources indicate that while they excel in mobility work, don't expect crazy heavy resistance. They come in five resistance levels, from 'very light' to 'very heavy', ranging from 3 to 27 pounds. The various levels also differ in length, ranging from the 44-inch very light cord to the very heavy 53-inch cord, so you can pick the size and tension right for you.

If you want to go all in with resistance bands, WHATAFIT offers five bands (10, 20, 30, 40, 50-pound listed resistances), handles, ankle straps, a door anchor, and a carrying pouch. Some bundles even come with additional looped or mini bands. You’re not going to get much closer to having a complete gym in your home—especially for under $40—than with this set.

Industry observers note that the set is also wildly popular: With a 4.6-star average and over 34,000 reviews—more than any other band on this list—it has the people’s approval. You can stack the bands for more precise resistance, which makes progressive overload easier and mimics the flexibility you’d get in a commercial gym. As one reviewer put it: “The materials feel high-quality and durable, and the bands have held up really well so far. I’ve used them for upper body, lower body, and core training without any issues. Plus, the whole set is compact and easy to store or travel with.”.

It has been revealed that what holds it back slightly is that these bands are serviceable, not premium. While natural latex is great for elasticity, it can degrade over time with sweat, sun, and repeated stretch cycles, so expect some wear. That mentioned, for the price, this set offers a wide breadth of use and works well for someone building up strength or who needs a versatile “one-stop” band kit.

Your most important consideration should be how you strategy to use your resistance bands—for solo workouts, to add resistance to exercises, to help you with dips or pull-ups, or to warm up before your lifts. No one band will perfectly check every box.

It has been revealed that most resistance bands are made from latex and rubber (or some combination of the two) and use plastic parts for accessories like handles and door anchors. (If you have a latex allergy, there are latex-free resistance bands.) So we’re not going to list materials as a significant consideration.

Likewise, the bands in this guide are all similar in price, with no major outliers. Premium and/or unique band designs cost more, but expect to pay between $20 and $70 for bands. The price scales based on the band resistance and whether or not you’re buying a set. Below are the top three things you should consider when shopping around for a latest resistance band.

The type of band you buy dictates the kind of workouts you can perform. Here’s a quick breakdown of the band styles you’ll see, save for a few unique models, most of which are on this list.

In a recent development, also referred to as super bands, these are the quintessential resistance bands that most manufacturers sell. Because the band is a single loop, you have to get creative in performing specific exercises, but you can target most major muscles with a looped band. You can also wrap them around pull-up bars, barbells, and machines to change the resistance profile of an exercise.

It has been revealed that popular in physical therapy offices, mini bands are an excellent tool for activating the smaller muscles in your hips, legs, upper back, and shoulders. They can’t support your bodyweight and they don’t stretch far enough to allow for squats, presses, or curls. Think of these as a warm-up tool, not a workout replacement.

These bands are defined by a single tube of rubber with a handle on each end (usually). These bands give you the most freedom of movement, and the handles allow you to press and row more efficiently (compared to looped bands).

Industry observers note that some bands cite a single poundage versus a range. If a band lists its resistance as between 20 and 60 force, you’ll experience 20 pounds of resistance when the band is least stretched and 60 pounds at the most stretched position. Squatting with a 50-pound band doesn’t feel the same as squatting with a 50-pound dumbbell, either, since the force you’re resisting is literally changing with every inch you move.

To track your progress effectively, find a band that has you reaching within one to three reps of failure for your desired rep range. Stick with that band until the reps feel easier, and then move up to the next heaviest band you have. Progressing with bands isn’t as easy as with free weights and machines, but you'll make gains as long as you’re basing your effort on training intensity and not weight.

Resistance bands can be dangerous. If they snap while doing assisted pull-ups or a face pull, you’ll fall or injure your eyes or face. No band is wear-proof, so it’s essential to use them responsibly: don’t overstretch, inspect them regularly for tears, and avoid anchoring them against textured surfaces like the knurling on a barbell, which creates friction that weakens the material.

Manufacturers use different strategies to improve longevity. Some bands are built from layered latex for added reinforcement, while others encase the elastic in a protective sleeve that reduces wear and shields the user from a whip-like snap mid-rep. These features can’t eliminate risk, but they can extend the lifespan of your bands and make training safer.

As a longtime fitness journalist and NASM-certified trainer, I have spent years using resistance bands in a variety of exercise scenarios. For this story, I worked in tandem with the team at Men's Health, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, and Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. We also recruited the help of MH Strength in Diversity members Juan Guadarrama, CSCS and Eric Sung, CSCS to gather diverse perspectives on the topic.

Recent findings suggest that we used our collective experience to put together a testing pool by putting the most popular designs that we could put up against upcoming offerings from classic brands as well as newcomers to the market. Both historically and in the pursuit of this story, we used these designs during band-only workouts, athletic movements, and to advance fundamental movements like the deadlift. The selections above represent the best resistance bands that you can buy now.

We asked Strength in Diversity member Eric Sung about his favorite ways to incorporate resistance bands with clients and in his own training.

"The banded rear delt fly is great exercise to do as a warm up to prepare your body before an upper body session," states Sung. "Grab the band, hold it out in front of you, stretch it across your upper chest and try to resist the band as much and slowly as you can.".

If you're looking to get started in training lower body plyometrics, put band-assisted squat jumps on your radar. "Tie a band to a high anchor, grab each end of it, assume your squat stance, and focus on jumping as high as you can with the assistance of the band. This is a great entry point," he adds.

For more ideas, check out our list of 12 resistance band workouts you can do at home.

In a recent development, similar to free weights, resistance bands help create tension and place stress on the muscles, explains Sung. However, resistance bands assist in efforts to build muscle and strength in a few unique ways.

Sources indicate that because they deliver more resistance as you stretch them further, they offer a different challenge than free weights. This means your muscles face the most load and tension at the top of every exercise. For example, the top of a resistance band pushup is a challenge; the top of a bodyweight pushup is a position of rest.

It has been revealed that another way resistance bands help build strength is by assisting in movements that an individual cannot yet complete at baseline standards, explains Guadarrama. "It allows athletes to move through the full range of motion and acquire neuromuscular capacity," he explains. "Over time the body can adapt, learn the movement, and build the strength needed for the unassisted effort.".

Bands can also be attached to plates and kettlebells to add more resistance to the eccentric or concentric phases of a given movement, explains Guadarrama. "Each of these methods has benefits to biomechanical advantages and providing variance in stress," he notes.

XRP has seen traders withdraw large amounts of tokens out of major crypto exchanges, especially Binance, over the last 30 days even as the broad market volatility persists.

Despite the intense selling pressure XRP has witnessed over the past few months, data from the crypto analytics platform Cryptoquant demonstrates that XRP’s exchange outflow has reached 5 billion XRP over the last month.

While the massive 30-day exchange outflow of 5 billion XRP is a relief signal because it signals persistent demand for XRP even amid the intense volatility, further data shows that the outflow is relatively low compared to levels seen in October.

Although the 5 billion XRP outflow is significant and November has yet to wrap up, the data demonstrates that it marks a decent decrease from October, when total exchange outflows for the month reached about 5.7 billion XRP.

Despite the 700,000 XRP decrease in the metric, the outflows registered in the last 30 days are still considered substantial and have drawn attention from market analysts as they signal strong investor conviction even as XRP suffered larger price losses this month compared with October.

Usually, increases in the exchange outflow of an asset suggest that investors are moving assets off exchanges into external wallets, most likely to hold them for longer periods.

Hence, this metric provides a bullish signal for XRP as it indicates strong demand among traders, putting Binance in the spotlight as over a billion XRP were withdrawn from the exchange during the period.

While OKX and Bybit saw traders withdraw 865.27 million XRP and 697.65 million XRP from their platforms, respectively, Binance registered the highest XRP withdrawals, with about 1.439 billion XRP leaving its exchange over the period.

Vitamin C May Lower Your Risk of Cancer from Certain Processed Foods

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer.
  • In a recent development, now, new research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer. Specifically, once they hit your stomach, nitrates and nitrites found in these foods can spark a chain reaction called nitrosation that allows carcinogens to develop. This isn’t just a meat-eating matter either: fruits and vegetables that have grown in areas affected by pollution can also lead to this chain reaction.

In a recent development, now, new research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement. It can cut this chain reaction and, in theory, lower the odds that carcinogens will develop after eating certain foods linked to this reaction, according to the findings.

Recent findings suggest that researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon. But the findings raise a lot of questions about why this may work and how to actually put it into practice in a safe way. Here’s what the researcher behind the study and dietitians want you to keep in mind.

It has been revealed that meet the experts: Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo; Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; and Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

For the study, researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body, and where they undergo chemical changes. The model looked at a range of areas, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma (i.e. the liquid part of your blood). Researchers discovered that having vitamin C alongside foods that contain nitrates and nitrites may halt chain reactions that happen in the body, including nitrosation, which makes substances that are linked to cancer development.

It has been revealed that the researchers also looked at whether taking vitamin C after each meal could help, and found that it may reduce the formation of nitrosation products linked with cancer risk. The boost was most meaningful when people had foods that contained nitrates and nitrites, like salami, bacon, and other processed meats.

The researchers also theorized that this may explain why certain types of produce that happen to contain both vitamin C and nitrates (like spinach) don’t seem to increase cancer risk, while others do.

According to recent reports, it’s notable to stress this: The study was based on a mathematical model and was not a clinical trial or data analysis. Because of that, it's hard to draw too many conclusions right now.

Still, this link isn’t out of nowhere. “Under acidic conditions in the stomach, nitrites can undergo chemical reactions that lead to the formation of potentially harmful N-nitroso compounds,” states Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo. “Vitamin C can interfere with these reactions, reducing the formation of these compounds.”.

Why vitamin C? “Vitamin C is an antioxidant,” points out Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. Meaning, it helps to neutralize unstable molecules in the body—and may do the same for nitrosation.

But the effectiveness of vitamin C depends on when it’s in the stomach compared to when these reactions happen, McNicol adds. “Our simulations suggest that taking vitamin C shortly after meals could be particularly effective, as this allows vitamin C to overlap more closely with periods when nitrosation would otherwise be relatively high,” he says.

Experts stress that it’s crucial to keep the study in perspective. “While the findings are promising, more research is needed to determine whether taking vitamin C after meals actually reduces cancer risk,” notes Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

Cording agrees, stressing that while the findings are “promising,” they’re still just based on a mathematical model at this point. “That remarked, getting enough vitamin C and other antioxidants, alongside nutrients like fiber and other beneficial plant compounds, has been associated with reduced risk of disease and with overall immune system function,” Cording says. “There are lots of great reasons to include vitamin-C rich fruits and vegetables throughout the day.”.

There are other things to consider, like practicality and safety. “Our research does not establish that taking vitamin C supplements after every meal is necessary or advisable,” McNicol claims. “Although our simulations suggest that dividing a fixed daily supplement across meals may be more effective than taking the same amount at once, further experimental and clinical studies are needed to determine whether these strategies are effective and safe in people.”.

High doses of vitamin C from supplements can also lead to GI discomfort, including nausea and diarrhea, Gans points out.

According to recent reports, for now, this is more of an interesting finding vs. an actual dietary recommendation. “Until we have more research, there's no reason to recommend intentionally adding extra vitamin C, whether from food or supplements, after every meal specifically to reduce cancer risk,” Gans says.

In a recent development, carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

Recent findings suggest that she began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

In a recent development, carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

PQC algorithms deliver the same core functions like regular cryptography, but absorb the quantum-computing hazards.

SWIFT, the largest European financial conglomerate, has just released their latest perspective on quantum computing threats, a topic the crypto community, including the XRP Army, has eagerly debated over the past few months.

The financial community is uniting towards building the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) service, which would replace the algorithms prone to breaking by quantum computing. This aligns with the roadmap of several DLT-based altcoins, including Ripple (XRP) & Algorand (ALGO).

Sources indicate that both of these Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) based chains are preparing for signatures that erases those threats, potentially fully implementing it by 2028. “Today’s cryptography is deeply embedded across systems, applications & processes”, – the paper states, carving out a transitional path.

In a recent development, transitioning to new standards requires SWIFT compliant organisations to understand where they are exposed and manage change in a controlled, resilient way. Blockchain adoption comes as a no-brainer: SWIFT’s new ledger acts as a plug between multiple popular chains, including Ripple’s XRP.

In a recent development, Q-Day is coming. Are we ready?Quantum computing could reshape the foundations of financial security as we know them.Preparing for that future starts now, and it will take the financial community working together.In the latest article in our Perspectives series, Michael… pic.twitter.com/kjLteDKFeM.

Recent findings suggest that SWIFT’s statement urges companies not to wait for complete inventory of cryptographic assets, but rather prioritise their most critical and exposed systems, beginning the PQC transition. That’s where Algorand (ALGO) & Ripple’s XRP Ledger stands out from the regular crypto crowd. Algorand’s is leading the pack.

The chain’s workable quantum-proof mechanics are being gradually implemented from 2022, targeting broad quantum resilience by the last quarter of 2027. This includes more account features, multisig & solid research into a post-quantum VRF and consensus messaging. First Falcon-protected transfers hit the mainnet in 2025.

Sources indicate that it already protects historical state and offers native quantum-resistant accounts that people can use today. On XRP’s part, the Ledger sports a well-documented, institution-oriented initiative with a practical migration path (keeping the same address, dropping the old key) with a mid 2028 goal. However, that’s still pre-development aspirations.

🚨 Many people may not truly grasp the full picture when it comes to SWIFT!Why do people keep linking various cryptocurrencies to SWIFT?Here’s the key: the logic centers on three distinct roles:🔥 XRP = LiquidityFacilitates the flow of funds, enabling the rapid transfer of… pic.twitter.com/hh4a1zhj0w.

Industry observers note that algorand’s better matched with SWIFT POC aspirations for now. XRP currently uses classical elliptic-curve signatures, known as secp256k1 / Ed25519. No post-quantum signatures are live on the Ledger’s mainnet. The high-standard approach is going to be tested in 2027, while SWIFT is already piloting a roster of Ripple-linked banks.

In a recent development, santander, Standard Chartered, HSBC & Deutsche Bank are the highlights of a double-digit list, but that doesn’t necessarily mean XRP coin is used as collateral or settlement. The chain’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) provides an additional liquidity layer via XRP, but it’s optional.

The bigger question is whether XRP can become a standard settlement layer on cross-border corridors.

It has been revealed that set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate. The view from the bedroom into the living room.

Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.

Just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him. Covering walls are the many 20th-century figurative paintings Green has gathered over the years, among them Social Realist portraits by Raphael Soyer, nudes both bold and tentative, and myriad depictions of introspective souls—images that captured Green in a spiritual grip.

According to recent reports, he displays the varied mix in interiors conceived with his friend Dylan Bailey, the New York–based artist and set designer, whom he met years ago on a shoot. Their collaboration was informal. Green would come home and find paint swatches left by Bailey, who might pop by and hang up a work while Green was shooting. The furniture they found at auction. “I wanted to have matching couches so when a friend comes over we can both take one, sink in, and talk,” states Green. The vintage sofas’ peach upholstery fits right in. “I didn’t realize until after getting them that the color highlighted up in several of the paintings,” Green says, referring to a portrait of an ironworker by Joseph Paul Vorst and a double nude by George Valentine Dureau.

A Victorian Renaissance Revival bed mingles with works by Maurice Grosser, Raphael Soyer, and Moses Soyer.

Green in the kitchen, surrounded by photographs.

Green grew up outside Grand Rapids, Michigan, surrounded by, as he recalls, “cornfields and dairy farms.” With missionary parents, unstructured days, and endless skies, he had the space and time to imagine a different life. “I knew I wanted to be a fashion photographer when I was 14 or 15, then found out I could model at 16,” he recalls. “I won the lottery. Modeling was a better way to learn than art school.” He moved to Newly introduced York City at 17, the first student to graduate from his high school online. “I had to be here,” he says simply. “My first year in New York I shot with David Armstrong. He took me under his wing.”.

Now in his mid-30s, Green splits his time between the Substantial Apple and Los Angeles with his boyfriend. On the East Coast, between shoots, he runs Latest York Life Gallery, opened in 2022 and named after the Chinatown insurance company across the street. His first show, dedicated to Baltimore-based photographer Steven Cuffie’s tender portraits of Black women, reflected Green’s devotion to his own medium and enduring interest in the variance of human faces. The 2023 exhibition “Sleeping Beauties” would blur the lines between Green’s life and work: Many of the paintings shown have come to reside in his apartment.

Green kneels before a bookshelf by Renzo Mongiardino in the bedroom, which is painted in a custom Benjamin Moore blue.

Sources indicate that portraits by Raphael Soyer and Leroy E. Mitchell Jr. flank The bedroom’s 19th-century French armoire, which reflects a view of another Soyer painting.

Industry observers note that an Austrian Art Nouveau chandelier hangs in the living room, which displays paintings by (from left) Raphael Soyer, Joseph Paul Vorst, Raphael Soyer, and Hermann Grom-Rottmayer. The walls are painted in a custom Benjamin Moore color.

Sources indicate that A 1949 self-portrait by Leroy E. Mitchell Jr., for instance, hangs in the bedroom. This was the first painting Green bought at auction, prior to which it had been found in a dumpster. Green’s research led him to Mitchell’s early life in Detroit, his community of peers, and his time as a teacher in Ghana. Meanwhile, one of Green’s most pedigreed finds, a painting by Thomas Hart Benton, whose 1931 mural of industrial workers hangs in The Met, stoked another uncovering. “I had gotten multiple paintings and then realized many of the artists knew each other or were friends,” he says, noting that Benton and Vorst were studio mates. It is like Green is uncovering a parallel life of creatives finding true kinship.

Sources indicate that green Crowned the kitchen cabinet with art, including works by Raphael Soyer, Robert Philipp, and David Armstrong. To its right hang photographs by (from top) Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, and Richard Avedon.

Framed family snapshots fill the hallway shelves.

Recent findings suggest that it is these serendipitous journeys into the lives of other artists that Green cherishes as much as the art itself. “I love paintings,” he says. Perhaps a bit too much? Bailey would tease him that every time he arrived there was yet another portrait to place. “The reason there’s one hanging on the mirror over the mantel is because I had no more wall space,” Green says. As he explains, his collection, like his life and work, is ultimately about affection. “You cannot be a good photographer without being empathetic,” Green observes. “I love people. I love faces.” He’s made sure that love is hard to miss.

As the total number of burn transactions approaches the 22,000 mark, Shiba Inu’s token-burning activity is nearing another significant milestone.

In a recent development, the number of SHIB burn transactions at the moment stands at 21,991, with only nine transactions to go to reach the 22,000 milestone, according to Shibburn. In total, these transactions have burned 410,845,372,884,899 SHIB.

This is a testament to the continuing efforts by the SHIB community to reduce the cryptocurrency’s massive circulating supply by sending tokens to unreachable wallet addresses. The tokens are sent to these dead wallets and are then permanently out of circulation.

Shiba Inu began with an initial supply of approximately one quadrillion tokens. Since then, over 410.8 trillion SHIB tokens have been burned, meaning that 41.08% of the original supply of 1 quadrillion tokens has been destroyed. But individual burns have very different effects. Some transactions are for relatively small amounts, while others remove millions or even billions of SHIB from circulation.

The milestone is another sign of the community’s ongoing interest in Shiba Inu’s tokenomics as investors look for developments that could create stronger demand across the ecosystem.

The daily burn rate of Shiba Inu has seen a huge spike of 443%, as the SHIB community continues its attempt to shrink the circulating supply of the cryptocurrency.

In a recent development, A higher burn rate indicates more tokens have been destroyed than on the previous day. According to Shibburn, 4.40 million SHIB have been burned in the last 24 hours, with the daily burn rate jumping 443%. This contributes to a total of 8.42 million SHIB burned in the last seven days and 322.85 million SHIB sent to dead wallets in the last 30 days.

Despite these cumulative burns, SHIB’s price performance still depends on broader market conditions and investor demand. At the time of writing, SHIB was up 5.60% in the last 24 hours to $0.00000364 amid the Thanksgiving holiday and down 6.45% weekly.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IN A WORLD where home workout trends change with the seasons, the exercise bike continues to stand the test of time. Its appeal lies in its ability to increase cardiovascular health through a low-impact approach, with limitless ability to take it up a notch. With a range of indoor exercise bike styles available, from air bikes to spin bikes and even recumbent bikes, it can be difficult to choose the right style for your fitness goals and preferences.

In a recent development, recent innovations in "smart" bikes have expanded the indoor bike market even further, offering a wider selection than ever before. So we leveraged the extensive collective experience of MH fitness editors, anchored by months of hands-on testing from certified trainers, to distinguish which factors set the top options apart from the rest.

Recent findings suggest that each of the bikes in this guide can help consumers burn calories and improve overall fitness, but certain styles diverge in fundamental ways. Spin bikes, similar to what you might find at a SoulCycle class, engage your core and legs, while air bikes require you to use your upper body as well. Air bike enthusiasts appreciate their effectiveness in high-intensity interval training and circuit-style workouts due to their ability to require quick bursts of intense effort. Meanwhile, spin bikes cater to a broader range of intensities, longer cycling sessions, and supplementing outdoor cycling routines.

Sources indicate that to help you select the ideal exercise bike for you and your home gym, we've curated a list of the top exercise bikes we've personally tested, fitting all budget levels. From the ultra-high-end Peloton Bike+ to the most budget-friendly options available on Amazon, we've got you covered. Continue scrolling to discover the seven best exercise bikes, according to fitness editors and certified trainers, but first, a few things to keep in mind.

Being the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health means I get my hands on every piece of newly introduced gym gear that releases, sometimes before it's available to the public. To build this guide of the best exercise bikes, I took stock of the bestselling bikes on the market and put them up against overlooked classics and newly released options. I used each of these bikes for months, during long rides, interval training, as a warm-up, or a workout finisher.

Over the years, Men's Health editors like fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, as well as key fitness trainers from both the MH Advisory Board and the MH Strength in Diversity Initiative, have taken great care in researching and evaluating the wide pool of exercise bikes. Their insights were also integral in creating this list. Our team also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn to test and assess how well these bikes performed in a real-world scenario (read: a high-volume, high-traffic training facility).

Ultimately, we ended up with the below guide that represents our top picks for the best exercise bikes we recommend buying now.

Sources indicate that this newly introduced REP Fitness bike is one of the most impressive air bikes that our Fitness Director, Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, has ever used. “The eight damper settings create a ton of options for my training,” he claims. “And they essentially let the Strive simulate just about any air bike on the market.”.

It has been revealed that this Variable Pitch Resistance (VPR) system allows you to change the angle of the fan blades to give you that additional control over your workout. Most of us recognize the air bike for its impressive ability to make you suffer more the harder that you pedal it.

But with this latest system, the Strive bike gives you the ability to use it for steady-state and recovery rides as well as those brutal finisher and max-effort sessions.

In a recent development, “At an 8, this feels like a serious strength-style quad-pump that's harder per pedal than a Rogue Echo or Scwhinn Airdyne,” indicates Samuel. “That versatility, and the speed with which you can switch between settings, opens a new world of fan bike workouts.”.

Sources indicate that the Strive is also as sturdy as they come among fanbikes. Underrated: The cupholder is everything you want on a bike, suitable for small plastic bottles and larger metal jugs alike (and great for your iPhone too).

It has been revealed that this bike is no slouch when it comes to its hardware. In fact, it offers many of the same features as bikes double its price. From adjustable handlebars to convenient dumbbell holders, 32 levels of resistance, toe-cage pedals, and a spacious touchscreen display, it boasts all the features you'd expect from a premium bike. And it's wrapped in a sleek, matte black finish that oozes style.

Industry observers note that the assembly is fairly easy, taking about 45 minutes to set up. The bike arrives in a box about 85 percent built with just the feet, handles, and pedals needing to be mounted. The bike has a nice compact frame and takes up the least amount of space in the home. The brand found a way to cut down on the cost by removing the expensive touchscreen and giving you a platform to place your own mobile device or tablet on, allowing you to follow any classes you want that way.

It has been revealed that whether we were sprinting or climbing out of the saddle during intense workouts, this bike offered unwavering stability. We never found ourselves wobbling or feeling uneasy on this machine. The elevated bullhorn handlebars aren’t just about style; they provide an elbow rest that we found essential during grueling climbs. It's a thoughtful touch that we found enhances overall riding comfort. The competition-style seat on this bike strikes a balance between comfort and support that other bikes we've tested in this price range miss the mark on. It's designed for long sessions, providing that Goldilocks level of cushioning.

This bike offers an all-around fantastic workout experience, especially for the cost, and is a great pick no matter your goals.

The NordicTrack X24 earned its spot here because it doesn't just deliver cutting-edge training technology to the user, it also delivers the world for those more adventure-minded riders.

Recent findings suggest that do you want to feel like you are cycling through the Swiss Alps or along the beaches of Hawaii? That's what the NordicTrack offers, and not just by showing pretty landscapes on its 22-inch screen. Unlike the other bikes in this guide that simulate incline and decline by adjusting the magnetic resistance, this one actually replicates climbs or descents for a more accurate feeling of winding up and down the hills of Switzerland.

According to recent reports, the setup is easy enough to do solo, but it helps if you have a person around to help you for some of the more involved moments of assembly. The bike is sturdy and robust, but also heavy, weighing over 200 pounds. So be sure that you build it in close proximity to where you are going to want to ride it, because it's not very easy to move around.

Like most NordicTrack equipment, the X24 comes with a year-long iFit membership.
