Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • Sources indicate that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a latest production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

Sources indicate that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

If you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we unveiled a first investment of around € 3b in a fresh manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the latest production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company notes it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

It has been revealed that the building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a proposal to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

In a recent development, giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the newly introduced hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

Recent findings suggest that and the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

Sources indicate that that’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

Recent findings suggest that this is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Industry observers note that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

Bitcoin’s $60,000 recovery masks a growing threat that could push its price as low as $29,000

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cryptoslate

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin recovered above $60,000 after slipping below that mark on Nov.
  • BTC rebounded to $63,000 on Monday, but subsequently surrendered much of those gains.
  • According to Talos, Bitcoin lost 7.9% over the week, compared with declines of 2.9% for the S&P 500, 4.5% for the Nasdaq 100 and 7.8% for gold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin recovered above $60,000 after slipping below that mark on Nov. 25, in a volatile week in which Bitcoin fell to around $55,000, its lowest level since September 2024.

BTC rebounded to $63,000 on Monday, but subsequently surrendered much of those gains.

According to Talos, Bitcoin lost 7.9% over the week, compared with declines of 2.9% for the S&P 500, 4.5% for the Nasdaq 100 and 7.8% for gold. Over 30 days, Bitcoin has fallen 25.3%, approximately 2.6 times the Nasdaq 100's decline.

Bitcoin's correlation with traditional risk assets has also strengthened. Its 30-day correlations with the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 and Nvidia climbed to 0.78, 0.77 and 0.68, respectively, roughly 1.4 to twice their one-year medians.

Galaxy Research noted that Bitcoin's recent struggles are particularly unusual given its September recovery above the 50-week moving average, which has historically helped identify the end of bear markets.

Bitcoin has since fallen below both its 50-week and 200-week moving averages, breaking a recovery pattern that had held since 2011.

Bitcoin reclaimed its 50-week moving average in September after spending 44 consecutive weeks below it. It held above the indicator for seven weeks, reaching a daily close of $86,521 on Oct. 4, nearly 48% above its June low.

Galaxy found that none of the seven previous recoveries that sustained the moving average for at least seven weeks later produced a upcoming bear-market low, even intraday.

According to recent reports, september's recovery differed from earlier instances in one significant respect. Previous recoveries after prolonged periods below the moving average followed declines of 76.7% to 92.7%, whereas September's followed a comparatively shallow 53% drawdown on a closing basis.

It has been revealed that bitcoin's subsequent decline to $55,100 on Nov. 21 prompted Galaxy to withdraw its October assessment that the bear market ended in June.

The breakdown shifts attention to Bitcoin's June 30 closing low of $58,525.

Galaxy identified seven completed instances in which Bitcoin closed below a bear market low that had held for at least 60 days and from which the cryptocurrency had rebounded at least 20%.

Industry observers note that all seven resulted in further declines of at least 17.1%, with a median loss of 51.8%. Applied to Bitcoin's June closing low, those historical outcomes would put the cryptocurrency at approximately $48,500 and $28,200, respectively.

However, another closing low would push Bitcoin beyond the historical duration of its bear markets.

As of Nov. 22, 412 days had elapsed since Bitcoin reached its record closing price of $124,824 in October 2025. Its four previous bear markets took between 163 and 406 days to bottom.

The current downturn has also exceeded historical halving-to-bottom timelines. The three previous cycle lows occurred between 777 and 912 days after their respective halvings, compared with the 946 days since Bitcoin's April 2024 halving.

While those timelines suggest Bitcoin is overdue for a recovery, its valuation and investor behavior point toward an unfinished bear market.

Bitcoin's previous four bear markets recorded peak-to-trough closing-price declines of approximately 93%, 85%, 84% and 77%, respectively.

Industry observers note that successive downturns have become shallower, but the largest reduction between previous cycles was eight percentage points. A bottom at the June closing low would represent a 24% reduction.

The divergence extends to Bitcoin's realized price, which estimates the aggregate cost basis of its circulating supply.

During previous bear markets, Bitcoin spent between 140 and 304 days below its realized price. It has yet to register a single daily close below that level, which stood at $53,205 on Nov. 22.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the proportion of Bitcoin's supply held at a loss reached 57% on Nov. 20, within the 55% to 61% range recorded at previous cycle bottoms.

Despite that financial distress, Bitcoin's 30-day realized losses peaked at just 3.6% of its realized capitalization in February, compared with peaks of 7.3% to 16.7% during previous bear markets.

Recent findings suggest that investor sentiment has deteriorated more sharply. Galaxy's proprietary Bitcoin Fear & Greed Index fell to 5.2 on Nov. 21, its lowest reading since June 2022 and among the lowest 0.5% of historical readings.

Yet the index has spent just six days at or below 10 during the current downturn, compared with between 12 and 57 days during previous bear markets, including the month following their bottoms.

According to recent reports, derivatives traders have also maintained relatively resilient positioning. Bitcoin perpetual futures funding averaged a positive annualized rate of 4.3% over the seven days through Nov. 22, compared with negative 24.5% shortly after the November 2022 bottom.

Recent findings suggest that as of Nov. 22, Bitcoin satisfied just two of the 13 historical bottom indicators Galaxy tracks.

The conflict between BTC's historical cycle duration and the depth of its losses leaves Galaxy examining two potential scenarios.

If cycle timelines prevail, several valuation measures point to potential support between $48,400 and $53,200. These include Bitcoin's realized price, its long-term holder cost basis, and the smallest historical decline following the breakdown of an established bear market low.

A bottom within that range would still represent Bitcoin's shallowest bear market on record.

However, a return to the valuation extremes that characterized previous downturns could push Bitcoin toward levels between $29,100 and $46,100.

In a recent development, galaxy is also monitoring US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products, which have shed 71,339 BTC worth $4.95 billion since October. Their holdings have declined to approximately 1.24 million BTC, just 1.5% above their July trough.

A break below that 1.22 million BTC trough, alongside a weekly close below Bitcoin's realized price, would strengthen the case for a deeper downturn.

Conversely, reclaiming the 200-week moving average at $68,159 and subsequently the 50-week average at $74,401 would move Galaxy back toward its October recovery thesis.

BYD is bringing its $10,000 ‘Great’ Seagull overseas, but it won’t replace the Dolphin Surf

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.
  • The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China.
  • With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

In a recent development, apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

Recent findings suggest that in China, the fresh Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

Sources indicate that the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s new Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the latest version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Recent findings suggest that even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

It has been revealed that inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The newly introduced setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

Sources indicate that in China, BYD offers the newly introduced Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

In a recent development, the current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

As a style writer who’s tested more bras than I can count (at different weights and sizes over the years), I’ve found that racerback sports bras tend to work especially well for smaller and larger busts alike. That’s part of why racerback bras have such a loyal following: they’re supportive, comfortable, less likely to slip around, and easy to style under a variety of workout tops.

This is especially true for bras with added features like underwire, molded cups, or a wider band, states Dani Read, a senior designer for luxury lingerie brand Cosabella. “My boobs lean on the larger side, so I usually go for sports bras with a higher neckline to keep everything secure (no one wants spillage mid-workout!),” notes style contributor Lily Wohlner. “So when I first got this bra, I was a little skeptical.” She wasn’t sure it would 1) hold her chest up during workouts and 2) provide enough coverage. But Wohlner was pleasantly surprised and found that it actually offers a solid amount of compression, thanks to the nylon and elastane blend, which lifts and supports without feeling flimsy.

According to recent reports, it’s become one of her favorite racerback sports bras and she’s consistently impressed by how well it holds her in during strength training classes. The cute, strappy back design definitely doesn’t hurt, either.

Another bonus: the fabric dries super swiftly, so even when you break a sweat, you don’t have to worry about visible marks. It feels light and breathable, but the support is legit—like what you’d expect from a more heavy-duty bra. One thing to note: it runs a little substantial in the chest area. Wohlner claims she probably should’ve sized down for a more snug fit. That noted, her usual medium still works, it just doesn’t have that extra-tight, compressive feel some of her high-impact bras do. We also wish it had adjustable straps for customizability.

Breaking: Chainlink jumps 10% as its Wall Street ambitions gain momentum on two fronts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chainlink's LINK token climbed 10% over the past 24 hours to $9.20 as the network deepened its integration with traditional finance.
  • The rally comes as Fidelity Investments filed to launch a spot Chainlink exchange-traded fund (ETF), a day after enabling direct LINK trading on its cryptocurrency platform.
  • Meanwhile, Chainlink has expanded its financial market data infrastructure to support round-the-clock trading and lending involving tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets, including during market holidays such as Thanksgiving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chainlink's LINK token climbed 10% over the past 24 hours to $9.20 as the network deepened its integration with traditional finance.

The rally comes as Fidelity Investments filed to launch a spot Chainlink exchange-traded fund (ETF), a day after enabling direct LINK trading on its cryptocurrency platform.

Meanwhile, Chainlink has expanded its financial market data infrastructure to support round-the-clock trading and lending involving tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets, including during market holidays such as Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, on Nov. 25, Fidelity submitted a registration statement to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for its proposed Fidelity Chainlink Fund, which would trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

Sources indicate that the fund would hold LINK directly, with Anchorage Digital, BitGo and Coinbase Custody safeguarding its assets. It would support cash and in-kind share creations and redemptions but would not stake its underlying tokens.

The filing came a day after Fidelity added LINK, AAVE and UNI to its Fidelity Crypto platform, expanding its customers' access to digital assets.

While eligible Fidelity Crypto customers can now purchase LINK directly, the proposed ETF would extend that access to investors seeking exposure through conventional brokerage accounts.

The consecutive moves could substantially broaden LINK's investor base. Fidelity serves approximately 57 million individual investors and reported $7.9 trillion in managed assets and $20.1 trillion in assets under administration at the end of September, making it one of the largest financial services firms in the US.

However, Fidelity is entering a market where investor appetite has weakened considerably.

According to recent reports, according to SoSoValue data, Grayscale and Bitwise's spot Chainlink ETFs have attracted $176 million in cumulative net inflows since their respective releases. However, the funds recorded net inflows for just one day in November, putting them on course for their first month of net withdrawals since the market's inception.

It has been revealed that daily net flows for GLNK and CLNK through Nov. 25. Values follow Maketo's displayed rounding and totals are approximate, and non-trading days are excluded.

Source: Maketo Chainlink ETF daily flows.

Industry observers note that the slowdown in demand, coupled with LINK's price decline, has reduced the funds' combined net assets by approximately 33%, from $238.2 million at the end of September to $158.6 million on Nov. 25.

Fidelity's extensive retail and financial advisory network could help revive demand, but limited fresh capital could also intensify competition among issuers.

With Fidelity yet to disclose its management fee or launch date, the terms of its offering could determine how effectively it competes with Grayscale and Bitwise for LINK investors.

Beyond expanding investment access to LINK, Chainlink is positioning its infrastructure to capture growing demand for financial markets that operate outside traditional exchange hours.

On Nov. 26, the decentralized oracle network introduced Chainlink 24/7 on its X account, a market data service that extends pricing coverage for traditional financial assets to weekends and public holidays.

The service builds on Chainlink's existing 24/5 infrastructure, which provides pricing for more than $1.6 billion in tokenized equities across six blockchains and supports platforms including Ondo, xStocks, Robinhood, and Coinbase.

Previously, blockchain-based financial applications struggled to value traditional assets when their underlying markets closed, limiting trading opportunities and complicating collateral management.

Chainlink's latest service addresses that gap by combining traditional market data during active trading sessions with perpetual-futures-derived pricing when exchanges are closed.

The infrastructure could support continuous trading in tokenized assets, derivatives, and prediction markets, while letting decentralized lending protocols manage collateral risks outside conventional market hours.

Aave, which had more than $34 billion in total value locked at the service's launch, is adopting the infrastructure through Horizon, its institutional lending platform, initially targeting tokenized US equities.

The expansion also affects LINK's economics.

Fidelity's ETF prospectus identifies demand for Chainlink's services as a factor influencing LINK's value, noting that the network converts certain fees paid in fiat currencies and other digital assets into LINK through its Payment Abstraction mechanism.

While Fidelity's expansion creates another avenue for investment demand, Chainlink's ability to generate additional fee-paying activity from always-on financial markets could provide a separate source of demand for its token.

#144615. Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and claims it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • In a recent development, at 11:43 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators indicates Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and claims it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

In a recent development, at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

It has been revealed that the SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Industry observers note that FHP remarked the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

It has been revealed that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

In a recent development, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it claims Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Industry observers note that most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

Sources indicate that so Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a latest record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

In a recent development, this is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

It has been revealed that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

  • Recent findings suggest that the secret lies in layered lighting, which involves a series of soft illumination sources working together in concert: A bedside lamp provides focused task lighting for reading, while wall sconces free up valuable nightstand space and introduce a soft diffused glow.
  • Sources indicate that dimmable fixtures and warm white light bulbs can be especially transformational in bedrooms that also function as an office or a hangout space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you’re trying to unwind at the end of a long day, turning on the “big light” is simply not the move. The glare of a way-too-bright overhead light is not only unflattering but oftentimes overstimulating. It can make your otherwise cozy bedroom feel more like a department-store dressing room, leaving relaxation a little bit harder to come by. The right bedroom lighting, on the other hand, can bring a sense of warmth, atmosphere, and visual interest to the space where you spend some of your most cherished downtime.

Recent findings suggest that the secret lies in layered lighting, which involves a series of soft illumination sources working together in concert: A bedside lamp provides focused task lighting for reading, while wall sconces free up valuable nightstand space and introduce a soft diffused glow. Floor lamps can brighten an otherwise neglected corner, and a beautiful chandelier or pendant light doubles as a bedroom’s focal point, even when the light is switched off.

Sources indicate that dimmable fixtures and warm white light bulbs can be especially transformational in bedrooms that also function as an office or a hangout space. Ahead, we’ve rounded up our favorite bedroom lighting ideas, including sculptural statement pieces, portable table lamps, and wall-mounted fixtures that usher in a sense of calm.

According to recent reports, for a reading nook, a work-from-home space, or just a little warm white lighting, a floor lamp can show off your taste without sacrificing functionality. We’ve pulled two designer-favorite must-haves for those in the world of interior design.

In a recent development, this 1960s model from Danish designer Mads Caprani hasn’t gone out of style since its release. The pleated shade, bentwood spine, and U-shaped cast-iron base make it one of the most easily recognized and iconic designs in floor lamps to this day. If you’re looking to make a statement about your style, this piece does just that—landing somewhere between studious and stylish, as in polo champion Nacho Figueras’s Florida home.

Another lamp for tastemakers, this design from Isamu Noguchi has made the rounds in many celebrity home tours from a minimalist Brooklyn brownstone to Troye Sivan’s modern Melbourne home. Commerce director Rachel Fletcher has previously named a Noguchi lamp one of her bedroom essentials. The reputation of Noguchi’s work and the unique style of his Akari lamps make this a design staple for anyone hoping to cultivate a modern bedroom.

According to recent reports, we love the look of dual table lamps to frame your bed and create a distinct visual space in your bedroom. It also allows your bed to feel like a conscious design choice instead of a strictly functional piece. We’re taking bedside lamp notes from this Portland home owned by the lead singer of The Shins and decorated by Jessica Helgerson. And, if you don’t want to do things matchy-matchy, any one of these lamps would look great solo too.

According to recent reports, we love this moody metallic option from Article for a midcentury look—and we named it one of our favorite bedside lamps after ample editor testing. At $149, the price is also right.

If you’re struggling to find a table lamp that plays well with others, this is a viable option from coastal core experts Serena & Lily. This comes in four beautiful shades, inspired by the Italian shoreline, and there’s even a touch of rattan for a beachy bedside table moment.

The Flos Bellhop table lamp is a great source of ambient light in this minimalist Barcelona bedroom.

A godsend for a bedroom with inconvenient outlets, these design-forward portable lamps bring both ambience and task lighting wherever you need them.

In a recent development, another favorite of interior designers, the Flos Bellhop table lamp is a great source of ambient light in a minimalist setting. These super-portable LED lamps have four dimmer settings, are USB-compatible, and can last up to 24 hours on a single charge. And, if you love the simple glass shape, they’re also available as wall sconces for a stylish outdoor lighting moment.

Sources indicate that you never know when you’ll need a little extra light, and the Poldina Pro can adapt to your ever-changing needs. The lamp pairs a petite silhouette with the clean lines of Italian minimalist design, making it a versatile fit for your nightstand, dresser, or reading nook. Without any unsightly wires to speak of, the lamp can appear as an intentional design choice just about anywhere. Its touch-sensitive dimmer lets you adjust the brightness and choose between three color temperatures.

AD shopping writer Julia Harrison, who tested the Micro version, appreciates its versatility for desk work and kitchen prep alike. She notes that the lamp “blends shyly and seamlessly into all setups that require a little, but not too much, light.” With approximately 12 hours of battery life, it’s an especially convenient option for adding a little extra illumination wherever you need it.

Wall lighting brings a warm dimension to the design of your bedroom and provides great task lighting for a bedtime read. While we love table lamps on matching nightstands, wall sconces bring an added degree of intentionality in their design, as seen in Walton Goggins’s guest bedroom and Jennifer Garner’s kid’s bedroom.

Sources indicate that available in 24 colors and with flexible orientation, this wall sconce channels the fun throwback design sensibility of Portland-based Schoolhouse. Not relegated to the bedroom alone, these fixtures can bring vibrancy to any space—as is evident in the bathroom of this timeless, edgy Massachusetts home.

A visible mending detail modernizes a traditional style, so the pleated lampshade remains classic without being too precious. We love to imagine this lining a long entryway, or on either side of a tall headboard—the perfect lighting for bedtime pages.

Linen shades are classic for a reason: They soften the appearance of a light fixture, giving even the most straightforward silhouettes a dash of warmth and character. Quince’s Contemporary Sconce pairs crisp white linen shades with a streamlined steel frame, available in brass or black for two distinctly different looks. The brass finish befits a more traditional bedroom, while the black feels especially sharp juxtaposed against pale walls and minimalist decor. Choose a single or double configuration depending on your space, or install a matching pair on either side of the bed for a polished alternative to bedside table lamps.

According to recent reports, if a flower could moonlight as a light fixture, it would probably look something like Soho Home’s Florie Wall Light. Inspired by the interiors of White City House, the members’ club in West London, the sculptural design features two gently curved layers of champagne-colored glass that resemble a tulip’s petals. A fluted, bubbled texture gives the glass an almost vintage quality, while the frosted finish diffuses the light into a soft, atmospheric glow. Even at just nine inches tall and nine inches wide, the fixture has enough personality to stand on its own, though opting for a pair to flank the bed would be an especially charming choice to imbue the space with a dash of romance.

Actress Laura Harrier hangs a bespoke pendant lamp in her bedroom.

The wrong kind of flush mount can be an eyesore, and the right kind of pendant light can transform a space from tragic to tasteful. These picks from IKEA and Lumens are both contemporary yet classic, proving them a satisfying finishing touch that makes all the difference.

Industry observers note that IKEA brings an affordable yet still-elevated style to the lineup with this ubiquitous, rattan-like pendant (technically latticed bamboo) from Ilse Crawford. We love this style as much for dining room lighting as we do for bedroom lighting. Can’t decide which? Two will only cost you $140 total.

Sources indicate that danish lighting design has a knack for making even the most practical objects feel like works of art. Case in point: the PH 5 Hanging Lamp. Its distinctive arrangement of overlapping shades creates a sculptural silhouette, with each layer directing and diffusing light. The three-shade system sends most of the illumination downward while allowing a softer glow to escape around the sides for ambient lighting. The result is a striking pendant that commands attention, even when it’s not turned on. The light would look especially beautiful suspended above a bedside table in place of a traditional lamp.

Supermodel Elsa Hosk incorporated a pink Tronchi chandelier, made of Murano glass, into her Fresh York City bedroom.

It has been revealed that might some consider a chandelier too much for a bedroom? Yes, someone who needs to live a little. A chandelier brings a sense of occasion to every space it’s in, and your bedroom deserves no less. These picks bring elegance without overkill.

We love how supermodel Elsa Hosk incorporated a pink Tronchi chandelier made of Murano glass into her Upcoming York City bedroom, and you can find a similar pick on 1stDibs if you want to sleep in rose-colored bliss.

Often referred to as the “boob light,” this type of flush mount can get a bad rap, but West Elm has figured out how to make them shine. This contemporary ceiling light fixture is simple, aesthetic, and subtle.

In a recent development, serena & Lily’s Capiz Scalloped Chandelier has the delicate charm of a seaside find, with a little extra glamour courtesy of its antique-gold framing. Each translucent capiz shell is individually hand-set, creating a softly scalloped silhouette that feels like a piece of jewelry for the ceiling. The natural variations in the shells’ shapes and opacity give the fixture a beautiful sense of movement. Light filters through the overlapping layers to cast a warm diffused glow, making it an especially lovely choice for a bedroom where atmosphere matters just as much as illumination.

If you’re looking for guidance when it comes to your bedroom lights, it’s key to keep a variety of factors in mind. Do you do a lot of reading in bed? Maybe table lamps should be your primary focus. Do you have enough fixtures to keep the space illuminated but not too bright? Perhaps a floor lamp or two will provide that glow for you. Are you spending most of your time winding down and heading to sleep? Try a night-light or string lights for ambience! And, of course, you’ll want multiple light sources to get the look (and the vibe) just right. But don’t fret, we’ve combed the AD home tour archives—and shopping lists—for the best bedroom lights around.

I Used the iRestore Laser Therapy Hair Growth System for Eight Months. This Is What It Did to My Hairline.

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

  • Hi, I'm Bob Gearing or, as my buddies like to call me, "Beauty Bob." By day, I'm a well-SPF’d tech sales bro; by night, I'm a red-light mask guy who definitely didn’t think he’d care this much about skincare.
  • ON A RECENT golf trip with 12 of my boys, I figured the usual questions would come up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Hi, I'm Bob Gearing or, as my buddies like to call me, "Beauty Bob." By day, I'm a well-SPF’d tech sales bro; by night, I'm a red-light mask guy who definitely didn’t think he’d care this much about skincare. Every month, I'll be coming at ya with a real-guy perspective on beauty and grooming because, uh, nobody really taught us about this stuff. Questions? Hit me up @beautybob.

ON A RECENT golf trip with 12 of my boys, I figured the usual questions would come up. Most of them know I write this column, so I’ve become the group’s official grooming guy. I always have a bag full of sunscreen and a newly introduced formula I’m raving about, and by day two, someone’s asking to try my Papatui eye patches. (We’re all 40-plus and when this crew gets together, the whiskey flows, so the under-eye bags follow.).

Sources indicate that this trip was different. Between rounds, at the bar, even on the cart, the conversation kept circling back to one thing: hair loss. Old friends, newly introduced friends, it didn’t matter. Everyone wanted to know my blueprint, and what they could do, too.

A few were confused when I told them I’m not trying every single resource at my disposal to grow mine back. I want to keep what I’ve got, of course, but within reason. Once your algorithm knows you have even the slightest concern about balding, the treatments, supplements, and potions being hawked to you are limitless.

According to recent reports, however, your time is not. Because I love how my hair looks buzzed down to a 0, I’m ok to leave the days of a thick flow behind me. What I’m going for now is the highest return for the smallest time investment with the fewest side effects.

In a recent development, last year I told you I’d traded my minoxidil foam for a discreet red light dad hat that could charge up my hair follicles anytime, anywhere. Since then, I’ve tested a few other takes on the tech, including a completely different device from a different brand: the iRestore Essential, a hard-shell helmet.

The company says its helmet led to a 43 percent increase in hair count within four months in a clinical study. Yes, I look like Buzz Lightyear when I wear it and my wife suppresses a laugh every single time she walks in on me using it, but I’ve learned there's a good reason for the spaceman design.

When I started testing the iRestore, one thing stood out right away. The helmet only asks for 25 minutes three times a week instead of daily treatments, which some devices require. For a toddler dad juggling a tech sales day job with plenty of night commitments—plus writing a men’s grooming column—three sessions a week felt much more likely to happen.

Sources indicate that another difference is that iRestore mixes in actual lasers along with LEDs. I’m the guy who’s always chasing the tech edge, so lasers not only sound like an upgrade, but after eight months, I can also say the helmet seems to be doing the heavy lifting it promises. (More on this below.).

According to recent reports, it’s also surprisingly light for something that looks like it was built by NASA. And yes, watching the lights flash around the inside of the helmet makes me feel like something is happening. Placebo or not, I’m here for it.

Now the tricky parts. Lights tucked into ball caps are easy to wear anywhere: the subway to work, coffee shops, school drop-off. It can layer into my day as it is. But the helmet style is strictly for the apartment. I can use it while cleaning or watching TV; I just don’t really want to be rocking it with other people around. (Though never say never—could be a hit at next year’s golf outing.).

Sources indicate that the other tricky part: Unlike the red-light hat, the helmet has no built-in battery. You’re either plugged into the wall or into a separate battery pack. Because I’m rarely sitting still—I’m switching over the laundry, grabbing the door for a delivery, standing up to yell at the Lions, or chasing a 3-year-old—I’ve ripped the cord out mid-session more times than I can count.

It has been revealed that leave the battery pack on my desk, and it goes flying the second I stand up. Stick it in my pocket with the cord hanging loose, and it snags on the chair. The fix I finally landed on: running the cord down the inside of my shirt so it has nothing to catch on, then clipping the battery pack to my belt or my shorts. Massive Dad energy.

In a recent development, at first glance, red light therapy might just look like a bunch of red flashlights—it’s not. A review of seven double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of at-home devices found that people using the real thing saw a significant increase in hair density compared with those using sham versions.

So what’s actually happening up top? Red light in the 630 to 670 nanometer range “is thought to be absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondria, which may increase ATP production and cell signaling,” says Dendy Engelman, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. It essentially loads up your cell’s gas tanks. “The hope is that this pushes miniaturized follicles to stay in, or return to, the growth phase.”.

The iRestore Essential runs at 655 nm, right in that sweet spot, which is also where the clinical research is concentrated. Drift outside it, and you’re in less-proven territory. But even within the range, Dr. Engelman says many cheap devices don’t deliver enough energy to the scalp to make a difference. The Essential packs 120 diodes total: 69 LEDs and 51 lasers. The lasers deliver precision down to the follicle, while the LEDs cover the wider surface of your scalp.

It has been revealed that this is where the hard-shell spaceman design comes in. Light loses strength the farther it travels, so for every diode to deliver the same dose, it has to sit the same distance from your scalp, every session. A soft dad hat can shift, tilt, or sit differently depending on the fit. A rigid helmet locks all 120 diodes in place, aimed at the top of your head and crown. (Thankfully, a few vents keep you from overheating.).

Recent findings suggest that these specs are crucial, and you’ll notice a lot of nerdy-looking language with most red light devices out there. But not everyone has legit data behind it.

It has been revealed that “It’s easy to get tripped up in marketing claims,” claims Brandon Miller, a client solutions executive at Clarkston Consulting who tracks the wellness tech market. “They may be copying the design and hardware, but they’re not necessarily copying the same type of diodes or lasers. So when you think you’re getting a good product, it’s actually a dupe.”.

For example, a box that claims “90 percent of owners saw growth” doesn’t tell you much. How many people were tested? Was there a placebo group? Who paid for the study?

His advice is to dig deeper, because the category is flooded with knockoffs. Start with the FDA language on the box. “FDA-approved” is the highest bar, requiring extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing, and it’s also rare for at-home devices. “FDA-cleared” means the agency found the device is as safe and effective as a similar product already on the market.

That’s the label to look for; then check the specific model in the FDA’s database. “FDA-registered” or “FDA-listed” can sound reassuring, but they only mean the manufacturer gave the FDA a heads up that the product exists. Nobody’s reviewed it for safety or effectiveness.

Even the FDA label has limits. Clearance “reflects safety and substantial equivalence, not proof of strong results,” Dr. Engelman says. And the knockoffs are worse: “Dupes often don’t verify wavelength or power output.”.

After many hours under my iRestore, the schedule is still my favorite part. Every other day, 25 minutes, done. Though my head is buzzed, I still keep an eye on the border of my stubble. I don’t see any fresh loss, and my temples are holding strong.

Industry observers note that but Dr. Engelman notes that short hair hides thickening I might not be appreciating. “To the patient, it’s like watching paint dry,” she says. Her fix: baseline photos in consistent lighting, an occasional grow-out, or go to a dermatologist who can use trichoscopy for an objective hair count. Maybe you will see me rocking some flow in the future.

In a recent development, hair growth trials typically show modest gains over about 16 to 26 weeks, so Dr. Engelman tells patients to give it at least six months. And, don’t forget, the benefits likely fade if you stop.

According to recent reports, should you stack it with other treatments? Dr. Engelman frames devices as an add-on, not a replacement, since minoxidil and finasteride have stronger evidence, as do in-office PRP injections. Topicals can go on before or after a session. “When it comes to hair loss and attempts to slow shedding and support regrowth, more is more,” she says.

It has been revealed that all the experts I spoke with remarked you need to figure out why you’re losing hair in the first place. Miller says most guys assume all hair loss is the same. It’s not. Genetic hair loss, stress-related shedding, and other causes respond to different treatments, so a device that’s great for one might do nothing for another. A derm can tell you what you’re dealing with before you drop hundreds on a gadget.

Dr. Engelman says the best fit is hormonal hair loss, also called androgenetic alopecia or male pattern baldness. “It’s the only type with solid clinical evidence behind red light therapy,” she says. It works best on early to moderate thinning, while follicles are shrunken but still alive, and “It won’t revive follicles that have been bald for years.”.

Recent findings suggest that stress-related shedding usually resolves on its own within three to six months, so she notes your money is better spent on the cause, like checking iron, vitamin D, and thyroid levels. For alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition, the evidence is limited. And whatever your type: “Think thicker, healthier hair and slowed progression rather than a new hairline.”.

Next, look past the light count. More diodes sound better, but Miller notes it doesn’t tell the whole story. Check that the brand lists its wavelength (red light in the 630 to 670 nm range is what’s studied for hair growth) and the power of its lasers, not just a big diode number. Then check where those diodes sit on your head, because light that never touches your problem zones may not be right for you. Stick to the session length the device was cleared with.

Industry observers note that finally, pick the device you’ll actually use. None of these devices work if they live in a drawer. Ask yourself what you’ll realistically do for six months straight, which is the minimum most dermatologists say to give any hair loss treatment before judging it. Choose the schedule that fits your life, and let’s head to infinity and beyond.

  • The appointments show who will exercise some of the voting weight tied to early deposits of ZRO, the token that backs validator votes on Zero.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that layerZero named Kakao Pay and ZAN among the first validators for its Zero blockchain on Nov. 25 and stated Four Pillars would run validator operations on behalf of Samsung Card.

Sources indicate that the operators are slated to help confirm blocks when Zero opens to the public, a launch planned for Nov. 30.

The appointments show who will exercise some of the voting weight tied to early deposits of ZRO, the token that backs validator votes on Zero.

Under LayerZero’s staking terms, the portal automatically spreads early stake equally across the initial validators. Holders have no say in which validators receive it and no way to withdraw early.

LayerZero states its launch validators will span Asia, Europe and North America. Its Nov. 25 announcement names the Asia-Pacific participants and identifies Four Pillars as the operator for Samsung Card.

Validators check proofs that transactions were processed correctly and vote on blocks. A validator’s vote carries more weight when more ZRO is staked behind it, according to LayerZero’s staking guide.

The project’s February technical paper describes a design in which operators can validate without putting up their own tokens, and the network selects its consensus committee in proportion to stake.

LayerZero’s Nov. 25 announcement named these Asia-Pacific arrangements for its initial validator set.

Early stakers cannot choose which validators receive their ZRO.

Sources indicate that the announcement identifies only part of the validator set. The diagram does not size total consensus voting weights or establish signing authority, operating independence or shared hosting.

According to recent reports, equal-width connections represent the equal allocation of early portal deposits per initial validator under LayerZero’s staking terms. The named arrangements follow the Nov. 25 announcement.

It has been revealed that the announcement identifies only part of the validator set. The diagram does not size total consensus voting weights or establish signing authority, operating independence or shared hosting.

Industry observers note that layerZero’s staking terms define genesis as the private mainnet launch, which the terms expected on Nov. 23, and that was also the date LayerZero gave for the opening of early staking. For public mainnet, the tech giant says staked ZRO will be visible in Zero Explorer once the network goes live.

On Nov. 24, LayerZero said the LayerZero Foundation had completed 100 million ZRO in pre-genesis staking in two transactions of 50 million ZRO each.

The portal’s rewards calculator indicates 300 million ZRO in an illustrative scenario that assumes 30% participation.

A holder who disagrees with a validator during the lock has no option in the portal to redirect the stake or exit the position, and the lock covers the staked tokens and any rewards.

LayerZero expects unstaking to open by March 31, 2027, and says that date may change. Once unstaking opens, it can take up to seven days, so moving ZRO off Zero to another chain may require a later upgrade.

It has been revealed that layerZero describes a 1% annual issuance target as the basis for the reward pool, and the terms set an initial validator commission of 10% on rewards. A holder’s share depends on how much ZRO they stake, how long they stake it, and how much others commit.

Any rewards compound into the locked position, and the staking guide says validators will set their own commission after the initial period.

HRF Confirms Funding of Seven Bitcoin Projects for People Living Under Authoritarian Regimes

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) is pleased to announce grants from its Bitcoin Development Fund for seven projects advancing bitcoin self-custody, financial privacy, and education for people living under authoritarian regimes.
  • It has been revealed that one project translates bitcoin terminology into 21 African languages.
  • Together, these efforts help human rights defenders, journalists, nonprofits, and individuals hold, send, and verify their money freely under repression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) is pleased to announce grants from its Bitcoin Development Fund for seven projects advancing bitcoin self-custody, financial privacy, and education for people living under authoritarian regimes.

It has been revealed that one project translates bitcoin terminology into 21 African languages. Another mines bitcoin with surplus solar power in rural Nigerian homes, paying it directly to the households that generate it. Others build tools for people facing repression anywhere — activists who need to find and fix the privacy leaks in their bitcoin use, communities who need self-custody devices built from parts found in any electronics store, observers who need election evidence preserved before it disappears, and people who need to turn an ordinary phone into an offline Bitcoin wallet.

Together, these efforts help human rights defenders, journalists, nonprofits, and individuals hold, send, and verify their money freely under repression.

HRF’s grantees for Round III of 2026 are:.

It has been revealed that many people want to self-custody bitcoin, but in much of the world, buying a hardware wallet is too expensive. CryoBrick transforms feature phones into offline Bitcoin signing devices. Because it looks and works like an ordinary phone, activists living under authoritarian regimes can self-custody bitcoin while maintaining plausible deniability. Technical Director Apalok will use HRF’s support to conduct comprehensive security hardening and peer review, integrate Bitchat for offline messaging, and publish how-to guides, expanding access to bitcoin and the property rights it protects to a far larger global user base.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin’s benefits remain out of reach for many African communities because high-quality education resources do not exist in their local languages. Exonumia, an open-source project that translates Bitcoin educational content, is building a Bitcoin Glossary in 21 African languages. The project will coordinate a continent-wide community of translators through three in-person and 12 virtual translation sprints, where native speakers review and validate more than 250 terms. Because every term is validated by native speakers rather than machines, the approved terms give wallet developers a trustworthy foundation for localizing bitcoin software into African languages, extending access to bitcoin education and the financial freedom it offers. HRF’s support will see the glossary published as a free public resource.

It has been revealed that in much of Africa, democratic elections remain a struggle and most countries are not fully free. Exacerbating this, evidence of fraud documented by citizens is often lost because paper forms go missing and photos and messages cannot be verified. Pawavox, created by Nigerian civic-tech founder Jason Omu, is a platform that gives election observers and human rights defenders a upcoming way to record irregularities. Using Pawavox, observers capture short video or voice reports, each GPS-tagged and timestamped. This evidence is then published to Nostr, a decentralized communications protocol, as a record that is much harder for anyone to tamper with. HRF’s grant will help fund the completion of the Nostr integration and expansion across Africa, helping protect the integrity of the evidence on which democratic accountability depends.

Branded hardware wallets are a common way to self-custody bitcoin, but under repressive regimes, they can be expensive and attract unwanted attention. SeedSigner is an open-source signing device that owners assemble themselves from inexpensive, widely available parts, so there is no finished-device supply chain for an attacker to compromise. It currently runs on a small computer, called a Raspberry Pi Zero, which can be unavailable in regions that need self-custody most. Lead maintainer Keith Mukai will use HRF’s support to migrate the SeedSigner code to more widely available hardware, ending dependence on any single manufacturer. Then, more individuals under repressive regimes will be able to hold their own bitcoin without trusting anyone else.

Many users assume they gain financial privacy by using bitcoin, but bitcoin is a public network, and the ways they compromise their privacy are often invisible. Stealth is an open-source auditing tool that runs directly on a user’s node (a computer that verifies the Bitcoin network). It analyzes a bitcoin wallet using the same techniques that blockchain analytics firms employ, then produces a report with severity levels, confidence scores, and concrete fixes for users. The HRF grant supports lead maintainer LORDBABUINO in adding support for the main Bitcoin network and building packages for standard node kits. With this tool, activists will be able to better spot the privacy leaks they leave behind when using Bitcoin, before an adversary does.

Nigeria is one of the world’s most active digital asset markets, but the legal path to acquiring bitcoin runs through exchanges that collect troves of identity and transactional data. At the same time, many rural Nigerian homes are receiving solar electricity for the first time, but much of that power goes unused in the daytime. Strandedwatt, a bitcoin mining initiative, installs small open-source Bitcoin miners in homes, converting surplus solar power into bitcoin, which is paid privately and directly to host households. The next step, backed by HRF, will see Bitnob CEO and project lead Bernard Parah deploy 100 Jua Kali miners in these homes and publish an open-source playbook other communities can replicate. Meanwhile, households excluded by the Nigerian financial system gain a permissionless path to freedom money.

In a recent development, A commercial Bitcoin hardware wallet has software and hardware the user cannot inspect, and carrying one can signal to outsiders that someone owns bitcoin. Specter DIY is a fully open-source, air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet that anyone can build from off-the-shelf components and verify line by line. There is no purchase record, and the finished device does not look like a Bitcoin wallet at all. For activists in Belarus, dissidents in Venezuela, and journalists in Burma, it is a path to financial self-sovereignty. HRF’s grant to the Specter Association, the nonprofit that maintains the project, helps fund hardware costs, AI tooling, and vulnerability bounties, ensuring the developers behind a self-custody tool dissidents can inspect and verify remain supported.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five XRP Ledger accounts supplied 72% of one day’s trading volume in XRP against Ripple USD (RLUSD), according to XRPL.to.
  • According to recent reports, for a test of the next day’s order book, CryptoSlate selected the five addresses that led the Nov.
  • Funded RLUSD in the first 100 buy offers fell from about 63,925 to 8,805.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five XRP Ledger accounts supplied 72% of one day’s trading volume in XRP against Ripple USD (RLUSD), according to XRPL.to.

According to recent reports, for a test of the next day’s order book, CryptoSlate selected the five addresses that led the Nov. 25 session in fills of at least 1,000 XRP, then simulated removing their buy orders.

Funded RLUSD in the first 100 buy offers fell from about 63,925 to 8,805. In the model, the matching pool, a standing reserve of both assets, took most of a 100,000 XRP sale after the removal. A seller would receive about 3.3% less RLUSD than with the full sample.

Recent findings suggest that the last XRP/USD trade on Kraken was $0.94935 when the ticker was checked at 13:07:24 UTC on Nov. 26. On the ledger exchange itself, XRP/RLUSD accounted for 84% of all volume measured in XRP over the seven days covered by XRPL.to’s reconstruction.

According to recent reports, in the 24 hours ending at 01:30 UTC on Nov. 25, XRPL.to’s reconstruction counted 25,801 fills moving about 6.3 million XRP. Traders took resting offers from 142 accounts or traded against the automated pool.

The biggest account, whose ledger address starts with rpiFwLYi, supplied 41% of executed volume. Together, the five largest supplied 72%, and the pool accounted for 3%.

A replay through the public trade history endpoint yielded 6.32 million XRP and counted 25,712 fills for the same window, 89 fewer than the published tally.

The index can group multiple executions into one transaction row. In one row covering 525.58 XRP, the validated transaction showed about 514 tokens went to one account’s buy orders and about 12 tokens to another’s.

To test whether concentration persisted, CryptoSlate used XRPL.to records and split combined fills using validated ledger changes.

The comparison covered same-pair fills of at least 1,000 XRP in three 24-hour windows ending at 01:30 UTC on Nov. 24, 25 and 26. The same five addresses, selected by Nov. 25 qualifying volume, accounted for about 71%, 88%, and 79% of qualifying volume, respectively.

The address starting with rpiFwLYi led the middle session, with about half the qualifying volume. An address starting with rURtT5MM led the sessions on either side.

That left the same group with a large share in all three windows even as the leading address changed, and the turnover includes trades in which the addresses gave or received XRP.

The two sides of the XRP Ledger’s order book draw on different inventories. A resting order to buy XRP is funded in RLUSD, which the seller receives. A resting order to sell XRP draws on the seller’s inventory.

The relevant depth for a seller is the RLUSD that buyers can deliver at the displayed prices.

Recent findings suggest that at validated ledger 108584374, which closed at 13:09:20 UTC on Nov. 26, the first 100 buy offers could take about 67,549 XRP at the displayed prices.

Excluding buy offers from the five large-fill leaders left room for about 9,302 XRP in that same sample. The funded RLUSD in the sample fell about 86%.

Recent findings suggest that the matching XRP/RLUSD pool held about 1.99 million XRP and 1.89 million RLUSD. The model applied its standard 0.315% fee and allocated each portion of the sale to the better available price.

The test held the remaining offers fixed and used only the sampled book and the direct pool, with deeper orders, replacement orders, and additional fees outside the simulation.

Industry observers note that in the model, a 1,000 sale returned 947.96 RLUSD with the full order sample and 947.87 without the five addresses’ buy orders. At 10,000, proceeds slipped from 9,474.85 to 9,470.90 RLUSD. At 100,000, proceeds fell from 94,197.18 to 91,050.74 RLUSD.

The pool took about 32,451 XRP in the first case and 90,698 after the orders were removed.

A fixed-ledger comparison of how the order book and automated pool divide the same modeled sale.

Modeled proceeds fell about 3.3% as the pool took roughly nine-tenths of the sale after the orders were removed.

It has been revealed that the removal case excludes buy offers from the five makers that led the November 25 sample of fills of at least 1,000 XRP. The model holds the other sampled offers and pool starting balances fixed and excludes deeper, new and other-market orders.

Each bar totals 100,000 XRP. Order-book volume is that total minus modeled pool volume. Amounts and proceeds are rounded to whole units. The source inputs are the first 100 buy offers and the matching pool at validated ledger 108584374, with the pool’s standard fee.

The removal case excludes buy offers from the five makers that led the November 25 sample of fills of at least 1,000 XRP. The model holds the other sampled offers and pool starting balances fixed and excludes deeper, latest and other-market orders.

The pool’s price worsens as sellers draw down its RLUSD reserves, which is why a large trade can clear and still return less.

Pottery Barn Jake Leather Sofa Review, Tested by AD (2026)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I’ve wanted a leather sofa for many years, but I could never find a color I liked—a detail just as important to me as the material.
  • Industry observers note that if you don’t love the stately green hue as much as I do, that hardly means the Jake isn’t your room’s match.
  • Sources indicate that how much does it cost?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I’ve wanted a leather sofa for many years, but I could never find a color I liked—a detail just as important to me as the material. I wasn’t interested in the usual black, brown, or cognac options, instead preferring something less traditional but not squarely trendy. And then I discovered Pottery Barn’s Jake Leather Sofa in Vintage Hunter, which hit my sofa sweet spot, exuding a deep confidence that reads as rich, grounded, and classy. Its sophisticated presence anchors my living room without overpowering the space.

Industry observers note that if you don’t love the stately green hue as much as I do, that hardly means the Jake isn’t your room’s match. The sofa’s customization options—another major selling point—are robust: In addition to being able to choose from a broad range of leathers and upholstery colors, I could also select the style of the seat and back cushions, adding up to a piece of furniture that feels more personal than an off-the-sales-floor purchase. With its slim arms, low profile, plush cushions, and bronze-finished metal legs, it strikes a balance between streamlined and inviting.

Sources indicate that how much does it cost? Are there payment intends available?

The cost of the Jake depends on the size, material, and cushion configuration you choose, falling somewhere between $2,000 and $6,000 for most designs. To save yourself from shopping-cart sticker shock, price out the exact model you want, since the leather grade and sofa width can meaningfully change the total. For instance, my 86-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep model in Vintage Hunter retails for $3,999, but a 70-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep loveseat in a Chocolate Performance fabric costs $3,099, and is sometimes on sale for less.

What are the upholstery or customization options? Did you choose any?

There’s little you can’t choose with the Jake. Available in an extensive selection of leather colors and finishes, you can also pick the number of back cushions you’d like (two or three) and style of seat cushion (two separate or a single bench). For my vintage leather sofa in Hunter, I decided on one bench-style seat cushion and three back cushions.

What is the lead time for customization, manufacturing, and delivery?

It took about six weeks for my sofa to arrive at my home after I ordered it, which felt reasonable for a piece with customized upholstery and cushion selections.

What kind of couch or seating arrangement did you have before, and what drew you to your fresh couch?

Industry observers note that my previous sofa was a smaller turquoise felt sleeper from Mopio that I bought on Amazon; its blue undertones made it feel brighter and more casual. I loved the feel, but dog hair got caught in it easily and was hard to vacuum. This Hunter shade is deeper, moodier, and much closer to the sophisticated design I had envisioned for the room.

What was the delivery process like? What was the assembly process like? How long did it take, and how many people did it require?

Receiving the sofa could not have been easier, thanks to Pottery Barn’s included white-glove delivery service. Two people brought the sofa into my home, placed it where I wanted it, and assembled it on the spot. The entire process took about 10 minutes. For a substantial piece of furniture like this sofa, the luxury delivery experience was a major advantage.

According to recent reports, what are the dimensions? How does it fit in your space? Would it be better suited for a certain type of home?

I chose the 85-inch-wide version, which measures 36 inches deep and 32 inches high, and it fits my apartment almost perfectly. It feels generous enough to function as the room’s main seating option without commandeering the full focus of the room. I would recommend this size for a midsize living area, provided that the access points can accommodate its width. As always, measuring the doorway, elevator, stairwell, and turning radius before you click “buy” is just as crucial as measuring the piece’s final spot.

Sit test: Is it comfortable? Does it feel well-made? Does the couch have a tendency to sag?

In a recent development, comfort is where the Jake has exceeded my expectations. It feels supportive and substantial, and the cushions have held their shape without developing an obvious sag. In the four to five months I’ve had the Jake, several visitors have already stayed over and shared that they’ve experienced restful nights on this couch.

The only recurring quirk I’ve experienced is that the seat cushion occasionally slides forward a smidge. It is easy to nudge back into place and has never become a serious annoyance. It’s also entirely possible that this funky detail has more to do with my sitting tendencies than the sofa’s construction.

Is the sofa suitable for particular decor styles and if so, which?

It has been revealed that the Jake naturally fits with modern and contemporary interiors. Its low, linear profile, narrow arms, and metal legs provide a clean architectural quality, while the Hunter leather adds depth and character. However, with the right design elements in place, the sofa would also look at home in decidedly relaxed spaces, with warm woods, woven textiles, vintage pieces, or more traditional accessories.

Is it durable and practical in a modern home?

Despite its sophisticated appearance, this sofa isn’t your grandfather’s precious showpiece that exists for looking at and not sitting on. Rather, I’ve found it to be durable, practical, and comfortable to actually use daily.

It has been revealed that but that’s just for humans; pets are the bigger consideration here. I have a dog, and a few scratches have already appeared on the leather. My current remediation system is to cover the sofa with a sheet when we are home and remove it before guests arrive. It works, but anyone hoping for completely carefree pet ownership should be realistic about the care needs of a leather sofa before purchasing this polished piece.

Industry observers note that the Jake might fare better with children than with a dog, since typical spills are often easy to address rapidly, while claw marks are harder to reverse (if possible to do at all). I am planning to try a leather conditioner to soften the appearance of the scratches, though I have not tested it yet. Before applying any product, I would follow Pottery Barn’s care instructions to spot-test it in an inconspicuous area first. Ultimately, the Jake is probably better suited to a pet-free home, or to any owner willing to go whatever lengths necessary to protect and maintain the leather.

According to recent reports, do the photos do this product justice? Was there anything you were surprised to see IRL?

The sofa looks remarkably similar in person to how it appears online, including the depth of the Hunter color and the overall proportions. There was no unpleasant reveal on delivery day; the sofa I had spent weeks picturing was essentially the sofa that arrived.

Sources indicate that would the couch be easy to move into another room? Would it be easy to move to another apartment or home by yourself?

Industry observers note that while it’s more manageable to move than other full-size leather sofas may be, largely in light of its removable legs and loose cushions, I wouldn’t call the Jake a portable sofa. It’s not modular, but rather comes in a single piece, so moving it to another room or home is certainly not a single-person job. However, assuming the doorways and corners cooperate, rehoming its 85-inch span should be possible, so long as you have help on hand.

Comfort: A+Value: ADelivery and assembly: A+Style: A+Overall couch rating: A.

Morpho’s Steakhouse Prime EURCV vault on Ethereum showed 144.3 million EURCV in deposits and 107.2 million in displayed liquidity, including tokens the app could pull from other lending markets.
